judgment

THE DISPUTE

[
1
]

In legal circles, it is often said that where
there’s a will, there’s a fight, but that is usually because there is a second
will that is inevitably less generous to a plaintiff than the first.  What is
particular in this case is that there is no second will to exclude Plaintiff from
what she considers her rightful inheritance.  There is no need for that; the
first will does this quite effectively.

[
2
]

Plaintiff (“
Sylvia
”)
[1]
is the only child of the late
Professor Valentin Boss, who, by all accounts, was an extraordinary person both
on the intellectual and on the human level.  Defendant Krivokapic (“
Milica
”
[2]
) is Professor Boss’s second wife, who was over 30 years his junior.
The Impleaded Party (“
Helen
”) is Professor Boss’s first wife and the
mother of Sylvia.

[
3
]

Sylvia asks the Court to declare invalid her
father’s notarial will of November 12, 2010 (the “
Will
”:
Exhibit P-2
).
This would result in the succession devolving according to the rules of
intestate succession found at article 666 of the Civil Code
[3]
.

[
4
]

Under the Will, Milica receives
essentially the whole of her husband’s estate.  Sylvia would have received certain
benefits in the event that Milica predeceased him or died within 30 days of his
death, but those are limited to the revenue derived from the residue of the
estate, as stipulated in clause #3

3.  After making provision for all the
foregoing, my Liquidator and Trustee shall set aside and keep invested the
residue of my Succession for the exclusive benefit of my daughter, Sylvia BOSS,
and
to pay the entire income derived therefrom
to or for the
benefit of my said daughter, for her maintenance and support,
in such
periodic payments as my Testamentary Liquidator and Trustee hereinafter named
may deem advisable
, with the right on the part of my Testamentary
Liquidator and Trustee to pay such sums through such channels to such person or
person as he may deem advisable for the above purposes […] and such payments to
or for the account of my said daughter will continue during her lifetime.

(The Court’s emphasis)

[
5
]

The following clause of the Will provides for
use of the capital portion of the estate where the income from it is not
sufficient to provide the same standard of living as Sylvia enjoyed before her
father’s death, the whole in the “
uncontrolled discretion
” of the Testamentary
Liquidator and Trustee.  After Sylvia’s death, the remaining capital was to be
divided among four legatees.

[
6
]

In any event, this is all theoretical, since the
condition for her receiving any inheritance has long ago lapsed.  Sylvia’s only
hope, therefore, is to invalidate the Will, thereby leaving Professor Boss
intestate.  In that event, the provisions of article 666 of the Civil Code will
govern and Sylvia will inherit two thirds of the estate, leaving one-third for
Milica.

[
7
]

As for invalidating a will, there are
essentially two paths to that end: mental incapacity and/or undue influence or coercion,
in French, “
captation
”, a suitably evocative appellation for the
nefarious activity that it evokes.  Although either test will suffice to
discredit a will, a dissatisfied party will often attack it on both fronts, and
that is the strategy here.

[
8
]

In the present case, the Court does not share
Sylvia’s view that her father was not sufficiently lucid to execute the Will
and, accordingly, will reject that argument.  In spite of the fact that this
finding makes the claim of
captation
more difficult to prove, the Court
nevertheless believes that it is probable that Milica did, in fact, exercise
undue influence on Professor Boss in order to exclude Sylvia from any real
benefit under the Will.  As a result, we shall grant the action, and this, for the
reasons that follow.

[
9
]

In order to provide factual background for our conclusions,
and since Professor Boss’s mental capacity did decline in his final years,
dates are critical for our analysis.  Here are some of the important ones with respect
to his personal life:

•

Milica and Professor Boss start their
relationship                                  1989

•

Milica moves into Professor Boss’s house (“
[address
1]
”)                    2000

•

Milica and Sylvia first spend time together                            December
2001

•

Sylvia attends law school                                                           2003-2007

•

Sylvia moves into [address 1]                                                  August
2003

•

Milica moves into the basement bedroom                            September
2003

•

Sylvia is arrested at a demonstration and
charged                     August 2006

with assaulting a
policeman

•

Milica suspends working for two years to help Professor
Boss                2006

•

Professor Boss and Milica marry                                      February
14, 2007

•

Professor Boss diagnosed with prostate cancer                           March
2007

•

Professor Boss treated for prostate cancer                         June
2007 - 2008

•

Sylvia hospitalized in Mexico for bipolar
incidents                    February 2008

•

Sylvia is hospitalized in Mexico and then Montreal                   February
2008

for serious bipolar
incidents

•

Sylvia lives in an Ashram in British Columbia                               2009-2013

•

12, 2010

•

Professor Boss’s last semester teaching at
McGill                            Fall 2011

Plaintiff        December 6, 2012

•

2012

•

29, 2015

[
10
]

This done, we shall now turn to the two main
arguments advanced by Sylvia.

CAPACITY TO TESTATE

A.

THE STATE OF THE LAW

[
11
]

Article 703 of the Civil Code is the starting
point on this issue.  It reads:

Art. 703.

Toute personne ayant la capacité requise
peut, par testament, régler autrement que ne le fait la loi la dévolution, à
sa mort, de tout ou partie de ses biens.

Art. 703.
Every person having the required capacity may, by
will, provide otherwise than as by law for the devolution upon his death of
the whole or part of his property.

[
12
]

The Civil Code decrees that the “
required capacity
”
must be present at the time the will is made
[4]
.
Any mental deterioration of the testator after that is not directly relevant,
except to the extent that his later mental state might reflect on his mental
state at the time of the will.  This said, the burden of proof on the point has
been seen as being somewhat different from the usual case.

[
13
]

In that regard, there is a presumption in favour
of the capacity to testate.  As a result, the party alleging incapacity has the
initial burden of proof on the question.  The case law, however, speaks of a
shifting of the burden onto the opposing party once
prima facie
proof of
a serious doubt as to the aptitude of the testator is made
[5]
.

[
14
]

In this context, the reference to
prima facie

proof appears to have spawned a certain amount of confusion as to the degree of
preponderance required.  Our colleague, Marie-Josée Bédard, provides a most
helpful analysis of the issue in her 2017 judgment in the case of
Succession
de Charette
[6]
.
Citing abundantly from the Court of Appeal, she confirms that the evidence in
support of a serious doubt must meet the usual balance of probabilities
condition
[7]
.
The proof must show a serious, and not merely a simple, doubt.

[
15
]

What is particular about the
prima facie

test is not that the level of proof required is in any sense less but, simply,
that at that stage there is no opposing proof to contradict it.  The test is
still the balance of probabilities.  It’s a bit like the last minute of a hockey
game where the Maple Leafs have pulled their goalie.  When Weber intercepts the
puck at the blue line and shoots it at the empty net, it has to go into the
goal to count for the Canadiens.  It is still hockey, not horseshoes.

[
16
]

Accordingly, if Sylvia makes
prima facie

proof of her father’s incapacity on November 12, 2010, i.e., if she shows a
probable case of serious doubt about his cognitive ability, without taking into
account possible proof to the contrary, the burden will shift onto Milica to
prove on the balance of probabilities that Professor Boss was
compos mentis

at the relevant time.

[
17
]

As for the degree of incapacity, it is not
necessary to prove that the person was devoid of all cognitive ability at the
time of making the will.  On the other hand, to validate it, as the Supreme
Court noted, the ability to “
make
rational responses is not enough, nor to repeat a tutored formula of simple
terms
”
[8]
.  The
testator must be shown to have the “
power to hold the essential field of the mind in some degree of
appreciation as a whole
”
[9]
.

[
18
]

The following passage from another long-standing
judgment of the Supreme Court gives useful insight into the evaluation process:

Si le contractant, ou le testateur, n'a pas la
capacité de comprendre la portée de son acte, s'il n'a pas la volonté de
l'apprécier, d'y résister ou d'y consentir, si à raison de la faiblesse de son
esprit, il ne peut peser la valeur des actes qu'il pose ou les conséquences
qu'ils peuvent entraîner, si en un mot il ne possède pas le pouvoir de
contrôler son esprit, son acte sera nul faute de consentement valide.
[10]

[
19
]

Finally, in order to have a will invalidated for
mental incapacity, the party contesting it need not prove that the opposing
party was guilty of wrongdoing, undue influence, inveigling or any other sort
of improper behaviour.  The cognitive aptitude of the
testator is the test.  It is, nonetheless, true that
evidence of such behaviour can be relevant to the analysis, although it would
be more directly relevant to the claim of undue influence.

B.

THE PRESENT CASE

[
20
]

Before analyzing the proof, the Court must rule
on Defendant’s objection to the filing of Exhibits P-81.1, 81.2 and 81.3, since
that objection was taken under reserve.  These three binders contain in all about
125 pages of medical records from Dr. Elyssa Elman that Plaintiff’s expert, Dr.
Brock, obtained in April 2020 (the “
Elman Records
”).  Sylvia’s lawyer
attempted to produce them during Dr. Verret’s testimony on July 14, 2020, the
ninth day of trial.

[
21
]

Although Dr. Verret had previously received a
copy of them, Milica’s lawyer objected to their being filed on the grounds that
it was both beyond the normal delay for such a filing and, more to the point, that
Dr. Elman had testified in front of us several days earlier and Sylvia’s lawyer
made no attempt to introduce them through her.  Thus, at this later point, they
were attempting to introduce them through … nobody.

[
22
]

At trial, the Court took the objection under
reserve and permitted Sylvia’s lawyer to pose hypothetical questions to Dr.
Verret based on the information contained in them.  It is not clear whether the
objection extends to those questions and the answers they evoked but, if it
does, the Court dismisses that part of it.  It is permitted to ask hypothetical
questions of an expert and the Court sees no reason not to allow such questions
to be formulated using a document that is not technically in evidence.

[
23
]

The same does not go for the filing of the
documents themselves, however.  There is no excuse either advanced or possible for
omitting to file them within the normal delays and through the proper witness, especially
where that person appeared at trial.  In fact, Sylvia’s lawyer wished to
produce them without any witness.  He provided no authority for such an
exceptional request.

[
24
]

The objection is well founded and is
maintained.  The exhibits are excluded from the record.

[
25
]

Turning now to the allegation of mental aptitude, Sylvia argues
that, as a result of numerous physical and mental difficulties suffered by her
father starting some time prior to the signing of the Will, his mental capacity
was not adequate to allow him to execute a will on November 12, 2010.

[
26
]

In that regard, it is true that Professor Boss experienced a number
of often-serious medical incidents starting in April 2007.  The following table
provides a chronological recapitulation of those with some reference to other events
relevant to this file.

DATE

DESCRIPTION OF THE INCIDENT

April 2007

Diagnosis of prostate cancer

2007-2008

Radiation treatment for prostate cancer

June 23, 2010

Treatment at the emergency room in Cowansville

June 24, 2010

Transfer to Jewish General Hospital (“
JGH
”),
Intensive Care Unit, until July 2, 2010;

Diagnosis: Pancreatitis and Sub-Arachnoid Hemorrhage
and hepatic encephalopathy resulting in a period of delirium;

Discharge from the JGH on July 5, 2010

July 2, 2010

Move from the ICU to a general ward

July 5, 2010

Discharge from the JGH

August 6, 2010

Consultation at the JGH emergency room as the result
of a fall from his bicycle

Spring term of 2010 (Jan. – April) at McGill

Professor Boss taught two courses
[11]
and served on the McGill University
Senate and on the departmental Promotion and Tenure Committee, Majors
Committee and Honours Committee
[12]
.

Fall term of 2010 at McGill

Professor Boss taught two courses and served on the
McGill University Senate and on the departmental Promotion and Tenure Committee,
Majors Committee and Honours Committee.

September 2010

Professor Boss agrees to a phased retirement under
which he will teach in only one term a year.

November 12, 2010

November 18, 2010

Spring term of 2011 at McGill

of his phased retirement, although he continued to supervise graduate

October 27, 2011

and memory loss and a MoCA test was performed giving a result of 21/30

Spring and fall terms of 2012 at McGill

retired at the end of August 2012.

December 6, 2012

Professor Boss signs a deed of
inter vivos

trust naming Sylvia as beneficiary (the “
Trust
”)

January 30, 2014

Out-patient consultation with Dr. Howard Chertkow

Diagnosis of Parkinson’s dementia of moderate
severity, with possible Lewy Body dementia

April 2014

PET-CT Scan performed resulting in a diagnosis of
Lewy Body Dementia

September 18, 2014

Finding of mild dementia with Parkinsonian features

January 29, 2015

Out-patient consultation with Dr. Howard Chertkow

Finding of deteriorating overall condition

[
27
]

Focusing on Professor Boss’s capacity around the November 12, 2010
date when he signed the Will, the Court will consider the evidence under two
major headings: the medical/neurological and the social/professional.

MEDICAL/NEUROLOGICAL ASPECTS

[
28
]

The element that jumps out in this regard is the
bout of delirium experienced by Professor Boss from June 24
th
to
July 5
th
of 2010.  At that time, he had an attack of pancreatitis that
led to encephalopathy and delirium,
necessitating a 12-day stay at the ICU of the JGH.

[
29
]

The term “delirium” tends to evoke images of
mental derangement and insanity, and it is thus not surprising that this
episode plays a key role in Sylvia’s argument that her father lacked sufficient
mental capacity to make a will four months later.  In light of all the medical
incidents, however, the Court concludes that it is but one of many relevant,
but not conclusive factors.

[
30
]

Turning first to delirium, Plaintiff’s expert,
Dr. Jeffrey Brock, describes it as
“an acute confusional state often seen in the elderly with a concurrent
illness … acute ‘Brain dysfunction’”
[13]
.  In the section of his report entitled “
What is Delirium?
”, Dr. Brock
provides the following information:

Delirium and acute encephalopathy are essentially
different terms describing the same condition. The National Institute of
Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) has described encephalopathy as a
term for “any diffuse disease of the brain that alters brain function or
structure” and says the “hallmark of encephalopathy is an altered mental
status.”

[
31
]

Dr. Verret, Milica’s expert, speaks of delirium
in the following terms:

Le delirium ou état confusionnel aigu (
ou
encéphalopathie
) est un syndrome organique d’installation aiguë ou
subaiguë,
habituellement transitoire et réversible
, qui peut se
présenter à tout âge, mais qui est particulièrement fréquent chez la personne
âgée. C’est un mode de présentation d’une maladie aiguë, d’un problème
postopératoire, d’une intoxication, de l’effet secondaire d’un médicament ou
d’un ensemble d’événements combinés qui sont suffisamment intenses pour
perturber l’état mental. C'est la manifestation d'une souffrance cérébrale qui
se présente par un dysfonctionnement cérébral global. On en reconnaît une forme
hyperactive et hypoactive, certains oscillent entre une forme et l’autre
(mixte)… Le delirium est un syndrome fréquent qui se manifeste chez plus de 30
% des personnes âgées hospitalisées (10 % à l’urgence, ≥ 75 % en période
postopératoire ou aux soins intensifs). Ses conséquences sont graves, avec un
taux de mortalité d’environ 30 % et une morbidité importante : augmentation des
durées de séjour à l’hôpital, risque accru de déclin fonctionnel et cognitif et
plus grande probabilité d’institutionnalisation.
Ce syndrome se distingue
de la démence par la guérison possible de la personne atteinte si la cause
sous-jacente est déterminée et corrigée précocement.
[14]

(The Court’s emphasis)

[
32
]

The experts thus agree that delirium results in
a confused mental state, but Dr. Verret underlines that it should not be
confused with dementia and that it is generally temporary and reversible, citing
a third-party source to that effect.  Dr. Brock does not mention the latter
point, which is surprising.  It is a critical consideration in the context of
this file.

[
33
]

As well, in his second report
(Exhibit P-90.2)
Dr.
Brock details a telephone conversation with Dr. Chertkow only days before the
beginning of the trial.  In his recounting, Dr. Brock uses the term “
out of proportion delirium
”
[15]
.  This is a new characterization, one that is found neither in his
first report
(Exhibit P-90.1)
, nor in any of Dr. Chertkow’s comments in reply, nor in any other
document in the medical proof that the Court reviewed
[16]
.

[
34
]

One cannot help but suspect that this is an
effort by this expert to colour the facts, which brings us to the analysis of
Milica’s request to reject Dr. Brock’s opinions.

The challenge to Plaintiff’s expert reports

[
35
]

In her Notes and Authorities
[17]
, Milica poses four challenges to the admissibility of Dr. Brock’s
two opinions, being:

a)

The
failure of Plaintiff and Dr. Brock to respect the obligatory requirements of
the Code of Civil Procedure: Article 235 C.C.P.

b)

The lack
of recognition of Dr. Brock as an expert.

c)

Dr.
Brock’s lacking of expertise in the areas
sub judice
.

d)

Dr.
Brock’s failure to maintain any semblance of objectivity.

[
36
]

The first two technical procedural points are classic
“gotchas” that should never have become issues.  They typify the petty sniping practised
by both sides throughout this file and their mutual disregard for the principles
underlying articles 19 and 20 of the new Code of Civil Procedure
[18]
.

[
37
]

While it is true that neither of Dr. Brock’s
reports was initially accompanied by the declaration required under the third
paragraph of article 235 C.C.P.
[19]
,
this point was first raised in Milica’s Notes, which were filed some two and a half
months after the end of the trial and a year and a half after the first report
was communicated.  That is also where the absence of the Court’s recognition of
Dr. Brock as an expert was first raised.

[
38
]

Both arguments are factually accurate, but the
defects are of the sort that collaborative counsel should have raised much
earlier, to allow for timely correction.  In fact, the failure to raise them at
or before trial could indicate that the irregularities had been waived
[20]
.  In the circumstances, however, it was not necessary to rule on a possible
waiver, for the following reasons.

[
39
]

As for the Article 235 declaration, the Court
responded to the September 16, 2020 request by Sylvia’s lawyer for a possible
reopening of the hearing by indicating that it had seen no authority stating
that there was a strict time limit for attaching the declaration to the report.
Shortly thereafter, and before the last filing of Notes on September 25
th
,
the reports were refiled with the declaration attached.  There was no subsequent
objection from Milica’s lawyer.  This satisfies the Court.  The reports will
not be excluded for that reason.

[
40
]

As for the recognition of Dr. Brock as an
expert, article 293 C.P.C., which dictates that the written expert report “
stands in lieu of (the expert’s) testimony
”, adds a new twist to this process where, as here, the expert is not
called as a
viva voce
witness, whether in chief or in cross-examination.
It seems to eliminate the
voir dire
on the qualifications of the expert.

[
41
]

On the other hand, since the typical expert
report includes a description of the person’s qualifications in the area, and
since opposing counsel, or the Court, can always require the expert to provide
details on his professional qualifications
[21]
, a
judge will generally have ample evidence on which to assess those elements and to
rule on the person’s qualifications.

[
42
]

In this case, the first page of Dr. Brock’s
first report
(Exhibit P-90.1)
provides information on his education and professional practice
since 1984.  In particular, since 2014 he is a treating physician in three
Long-Term Health Care Facilities for the aged.  On that basis, the Court will
recognize him as an expert in the field of medicine, with a specialization in
medical care for the aged.  It will not, however, recognize him as an expert on
delirium, which he states as being one of his “
professional interests
”.  The
evidence is too scanty in that regard.

[
43
]

This conclusion effectively responds to the
third challenge raised by Defendant’s counsel.  We find that Dr. Brock has
sufficient expertise in the areas
sub judice
to provide relevant expert
evidence in his area of expertise.  Judging from paragraph 32 of his Notes, Milica’s
counsel seems to believe that the expertise requested of Dr. Brock would be in
neurology, probably because her expert is a neurologist.  But Sylvia does not ask
that and the Court does not grant that.

[
44
]

This does not mean that he cannot provide expert
testimony in his area of expertise, subject to any other constraints.  Here, we
note, there is another constraint: the fourth challenge, i.e., Dr. Brock’s
objectivity.

[
45
]

The Code of Civil Procedure dictates at article
22 that experts “
must fulfill their
mission objectively, impartially and thoroughly
”.  In a
2015 decision, the Supreme Court had this to say on the subject in a Nova
Scotian case:

[32] Underlying the various formulations of the duty are
three related concepts: impartiality, independence and absence of bias. The
expert’s opinion must be impartial in the sense that it reflects an objective
assessment of the questions at hand. It must be independent in the sense that
it is the product of the expert’s independent judgment, uninfluenced by who has
retained him or her or the outcome of the litigation.  It must be unbiased
in the sense that it does not unfairly favour one party’s position over
another. The acid test is whether the expert’s opinion would not change
regardless of which party retained him or her
(reference omitted)
. These
concepts, of course, must be applied to the realities of adversary litigation.
Experts are generally retained, instructed and paid by one of the adversaries.
These facts alone do not undermine the expert’s independence, impartiality and
freedom from bias.
[22]

[
46
]

Dr. Brock fails this test in a most convincing
manner.

[
47
]

In addition to inspiring no sense of
impartiality, independence or absence of bias, he analyzes elements and makes
findings of fact and factual interpretations that have no bearing on his
mandate and expertise, as described below.  In so doing, he attempts to usurp
the role of the Court and thereby destroys his credibility and usefulness as an
expert.

[
48
]

In his Notes, Milica’s attorney underlines the
following alleged defects on Dr. Brock’s part:

34.  A reading of Dr. Brock’s report
demonstrates why no attestation as to objectivity was signed nor submitted to
this court. The report contains demonstrable evidence of an extreme lack of
objectivity that Dr. Brock brought with him to this case. His manifest and
self-evident role of
partie prise
emerges both from what he speculates
about in his report, as well as his demeanor before the court.

35.  What follows are the various
statements contained in the May 17, 2019 version of by Dr. Brock’s report all
of which, it is submitted, demonstrate to what degree Dr. Brock’s assessments
are biased and replete with speculations unrelated to the medical files of
Professor Valentine Boss.

36.  Extracts from the report:

•

“Sadly,
she (Militsa) felt a great urgency for Dr. Boss to execute a will
poste
haste

(sic)
, independent of the
upcoming gall bladder surgery.” (page 5)

•

“Effect
of MK’s (Militsa) close and tight control of Dr. Boss local environment thereby
limiting or masking a more obvious expression of his cognitive impairment.”
(page 20)

•

“…it
became vital for her to have Dr. Boss execute a will at this time for fear of
another episode of delirium which would further impact his greatly diminished
cognitive function.” (page 21)

•

“MK
(Militsa) is a well-educated woman of
Yugoslavian origin…”
(page 3), a
country, as the court would know, that ceased to exist in 1992.
(underlining
in the original)

37.  These statements have no place in
an objective report. Apart from the questionable insertion as to Militsa’s
origin, the other statements were not only purely speculative, and implied a
calculated intention to Militsa that, though supportive of Sylvia’s narrative,
as the court heard and read, is totally inaccurate.

[...]

39.  Dr. Brock’s obvious bias is all
the more evident when he came before the court to explain the “need” for him to
submit a revised report. On day 6, he came before your Lordship and admitted
that the report that had been previously filed was based upon “speculation”.

[…]

44.  Apart from the tangible bias which
oozes from Dr. Brock’s report, his physical demeanor before your Lordship also
spoke volumes. His zealous counselling of the witnesses, his attempts, through
the questions that he was feeding to Me Lavigne, aimed at attacking the
credibility of Drs. Chertkow and Schondorf, two (2) pre-eminent experts in
their field, his jack-in-the-box behaviour throughout the hearing, all
demonstrate, it is submitted, that the court was not in the presence of a person
offering an objective view of the subject matter but one looking, at all costs,
to collude in selling a narrative, no matter what the method.

[
49
]

The Court agrees with essentially all of this
analysis and, in addition to our own earlier observations, there is more.

[
50
]

Dr. Brock attended much of the trial, even
though the need for his presence was not obvious.  Although he was allowed to
be present, he gave the impression - the very clear impression - that he was
acting as a coach, as well as a cheerleader, to the witnesses and lawyers on
Sylvia’s side.

[
51
]

He jumped around the courtroom to whisper into

UNDUE INFLUENCE/CAPTATION

A.

THE STATE OF THE LAW

[
74
]

Captation/undue influence is a straightforward
concept.  It connotes fraudulent efforts by a legatee that convince a testator
to make bequests that he or she would not otherwise have made.  Again referring
to the
Charette
case, the Court agrees with the judge there who wrote:

[233] Pour vicier le consentement d’un testateur, les
manœuvres (de captation) doivent être frauduleuses et elles doivent avoir été
déterminantes dans la façon dont le testateur a testé.  De plus, il est bien
établi qu’il n’est pas illicite en soi pour une personne de s’attirer les
faveurs d’un testateur.

[32]

[
75
]

The party who alleges captation thus has to
prove on a balance of probabilities that the accused party is guilty of, in the
words of the Court of Appeal, “
improper
schemes, disgraceful devices, lies, slander, deceit and trickery, or deliberate
misrepresentations
”
[33]
.

[
76
]

It goes without saying that this sort of
behaviour would not normally be out in the open but, rather, would occur behind
closed doors.  As a result, the judge must generally take account of indirect
and circumstantial elements and see if they lead to a presumption of coercion.
The Civil Code guides that process at article 2849, where it specifies that
"P
resumptions which are
not established by law are left to the discretion of the court which shall take
only serious, precise and concordant presumptions into consideration
”
[34]
.

[
77
]

Thus, the Court’s decision will inevitably be
fact driven, and there are many facts to consider here, going back over a
number of years.  It is somewhat helpful that a great number of the relevant
facts are mentioned, or even documented, in the numerous and lengthy emails
adduced as evidence in the file.

[
78
]

Finally, the Court understands Defendant’s
argument that, where mental capacity to testate is found, “
there is very little room to prove coercion
or undue influence
”
[35]
,
citing our colleague Lemelin J. in
Thibault v. Auger
[36]
.  Nevertheless, as we allude to above, a person can have the
capacity to execute a will in spite of fairly debilitating mental issues.
Where such issues exist, although they might not be of a magnitude to render
the person incapable of understanding and expressing his wishes, they could
certainly serve as facilitators of coercion.

[
79
]

This comes up in Lemelin J’s discussion of
captation
[37]
in the preceding paragraphs of the same judgment.  After citing the
Supreme Court decision in
Tewkesbury v. Ouellet
[38]
, he
turns to Professor Brière, who reflects our highest court’s reasoning there,
when he writes:

Les faits de captation
deviennent cependant dolosifs lorsqu’ils s’accompagnent de
pratiques
artificieuses, comme l’interception de la correspondance ou le fait d’écarter
les visites, ou encore le dénigrement systématique à l’adresse des proches
parents
.  Encore faut-il que les manœuvres frauduleuses aient été
déterminantes du consentement; pour apprécier ce caractère déterminant,
il
faut tenir compte de la résistance que le testateur était capable d’offrir dans
les circonstances, par exemple alors que ses facultés étaient affaiblies par la
maladie
. Il est d’ailleurs arrivé fréquemment que l’on ait attaqué un
testament à la fois pour captation et pour insanité d’esprit, ces deux moyens n’étant
ni incompatibles ni contradictoires.
[39]

(The Court’s emphasis)

[
80
]

In her quest to prove captation, Sylvia inevitably
points to the role that Milica played in Professor Boss’s life after his health
started to decline and the degree of control that she either exercised or
sought over it.  In the above citation, Professor Brière suggests a number of
areas that are relevant to consider in that regard and the Court agrees that
these can display a pattern of activity that could lead to a presumption of
coercion.

[
81
]

To be clear, the Court sees no reason to assume
that a person with even excellent cognition could not be unduly influenced by a
potential heir.  One need only consider the extent to which requests by the
caregiver of a physically disabled and dependent, but totally apt, patient could
influence the contents of the latter’s will.  The cloak of influence can come
in many colours, limited only by human ingenuity and physical circumstance.

[
82
]

As stated recently by the Court of Appeal:

[27] It is true that (the notary) explained that she
had the sense that K. was exercising her free will. However, before the trial
judge,
the issue was not whether K. intended to disinherit M., Sh. and D.
to the benefit of Ma., but rather why K. made that decision
.
Therefore, the trial judge did not err when she referred to
Mtre Bolduc’s testimony to conclude that Ma.’s untruthful representations
caused her mother to sign a will without free will, by convincing her that her
family was acting against her father’s wishes.
[40]

(The Court’s emphasis)

1.  THE EXCLUSION OF SYLVIA UNDER THE WILL

[
99
]

It is surprising, but certainly not unheard of,
to see a father exclude his only child from his will.  For such a thing to
happen, one would expect to see evidence of major confrontations and blow-ups
between two, or out-of-the-ordinary acts of cruelty or dishonesty on the part
of the son or daughter, or some other behaviour that would justify such a
strong renunciation of the normal parent-child bond.

[
100
]

There is nothing of that here, although there is no denying that
Sylvia must have severely tested Professor Boss’s patience during her years of
manic-depressive episodes.  The manifestations of her illness would also have
been trying on Milica, no doubt even more so, since she had no blood connection
to Sylvia.

[
101
]

By all accounts, Professor Boss valued family relations very highly
and maintained close ties with members not only of his immediate family, such
as his mother, but also of family much farther removed, such as his cousin’s
daughter, Caroline Dieluweit.  Moreover, he clearly understood, begrudgingly perhaps
at times, that his daughter suffered from bipolar disorder.  He was an
intelligent and humane individual and he must have realized that her behavioural
errors were not voluntary.

[
102
]

It simply does not make sense that such a man would bequeath his
daughter nothing
[43]
.

[
103
]

Milica pleads that the contents of the Will should play no part in
the Court’s analysis of the case.  Citing our former colleague, Stephen Hamilton,
now of the Court of Appeal, she argues that
the Court should not evaluate whether the testator’s
bequests are right or appropriate or make a value judgment on the testator’s
bequests
[44]
.  But that is not where Judge Hamilton stopped.

[
104
]

Citing the case of
Savoie
[45]
, he notes that the contents of the will were
pleaded there as evidence that the testator was unduly influenced and lacked
capacity.  He saw them as one of the factors, among others, to assess whether
the testator must have been unduly influenced or lacked capacity
[46]
.  This makes good sense and will guide us in
our analysis.

[
105
]

In the present case, even where Professor Boss makes a gesture
toward including Sylvia, he does it through a sort of tutorship, rather than
through an outright bequest.  The result is that, in the scant chance that she
would benefit from the succession, she would never receive full ownership of
any of the assets.  She could do no more than benefit from the income generated
by the capital.

[
106
]

This is striking, but some protective structure is not illogical in
light of Sylvia’s serious and oft-times debilitating bipolar disorder.  Accordingly,
had he chosen to make a major bequest to her, it would have made sense to
impose some control measures around it.  What does not make sense, however, is
the fact that this man who loved his daughter would cut her off from essentially
any benefit from his estate.

[
107
]

The numerous emails, letters and testimony attest to the fact that
Professor Boss loved Sylvia and admired her talents and intellect.  One of his
best friends for over 30 years, Dr. Harold Rich, declared in his affidavit that
in a conversation in 2015 Professor Boss “
immediately asked if I had heard from Sylvia, as he
usually did during our Sunday get-togethers
”.  His
wife, Ethel Saltzman, declared that Professor Boss had told her that he was
keeping his house in Boulder, Colorado for her.

[
108
]

This is typical of the testimony relating to his feelings toward his

When

y
s with affection
,
and

a

i

109
]

Professor Boss went to great lengths to aid her, in his own way
[47]

[
110
]

[48]
, whose

]

based on what she sees as a mistruth about an irrelevant point relating to who

Why would Professor Boss treat his daughter the way he did in the Will,
effectively disinheriting her?

[
113
]

Milica argues that Professor Boss did not abandon Sylvia in the
least, pointing to the Trust he set up in 2012, two years after signing the
Will
[49]
.  Professor Boss might have initiated the establishment of the
Trust, but the proof shows that the funds in it did not come from him.

[
114
]

Sylvia stated, and it was not denied, that those funds were left to her by her grandfather when she was a little
girl
[50]
and that Professor Boss placed them in a

[
115
]

In any event, these funds did not come from him and the Court
concludes that, given the terms of the Will, Professor Boss did, in fact and in
law, exclude his daughter from any real benefit arising from his assets.  We
also conclude from a
prima facie
viewpoint that, in light of his true
paternal affection for Sylvia, for him to do that was so out of the ordinary
that one must seek an explanation for this elsewhere than in his head and in

Milica.  No others seem plausible.

2.  MILICA’S ATTITUDE TOWARDS SYLVIA

[
116
]

In reply to a question as to whether she ever made negative comments
about Sylvia, Milica candidly admitted that she was sure that she said “
something negative to someone
” about her, but never to Professor Boss.  She explained that to do
that would have hurt him and her love for him was such that she could never
hurt him.

[
117
]

Taking Milica at her word on that for the moment, two conclusions
emerge from this testimony.  First, it shows that Milica was sufficiently upset
by Sylvia’s bipolar misadventures to criticize her in conversations with third
persons.  Furthermore, it confirms that Professor Boss was emotionally
connected to and invested in Sylvia, since his feelings would have been hurt by
any negative comments about her.

[
118
]

This said, Milica certainly made negative comments about Sylvia to
her face.  Milica’s July 2009 email diatribe
[51]

could hardly have been more disparaging.  Among other accusations, she states:

I do not
appreciate this message. You neither care for nor have you done anything other
than pay lip service to your
father's
serious cancer. Words are
cheap and actions speak louder than words. You certainly like words and are
verbose, but your actions have been few and the ones you wished to inflict on
him were ill-advised, badly informed, useless, unnecessary and detrimental:

[…]

I do not
trust you. You are an extremely violent person. I am sure that during your next
manic episode (and they have become more intense and more violent each time)
you would be capable of putting a pillow on my face if you were to spend one
night under the same roof with us.

[…]

You brought
stress into our lives on a continuous basis for many years now and you will
continue to try to do so, regardless of the cute missives filled with talk of
angels and good wishes. The best predictor of future behaviour are your past
actions. Michael Heslop and your mother are far away and do not need to deal
with your episodes, but then again neither do we, and I will shut you down and
cut you off as soon as I see that your phone calls and messages and actions
become stressful - they usually are, even on a good day. We do have some
rights, you know: inalienable human rights, to live our lives without your
violence, manic episodes and constant harassment - we too are human beings who
deserve a little peace and quiet in between cancer treatments!

[
119
]

There is every indication that Milica’s feelings towards Sylvia did anything
but soften over the 16 months between this message and the execution of the
Will.

[
120
]

Let us be clear.  Whether or not Milica had ample cause for the antipathy
that these words portray is not the point.  The law cares not why she disliked
Sylvia, or whether she was justified in feeling that way.  The issue turns on the
nature and the degree of intensity of her feelings and the likelihood that they
led to an effort to coerce her husband unduly when making his Will.

[
121
]

On another point, it is perhaps understandable that Sylvia was not made
aware beforehand of her father’s and Milica’s wedding in 2007, and that she was
not invited to attend.  Milica explained that this was a mutual decision
between her and Professor Boss because, given Sylvia’s unpredictable behaviour,
they wanted to avoid any untoward incidents occurring at the court house.  In
the circumstances, that could make sense, but it does not demonstrate a desire
to disinherit her.

[
122
]

On the other hand, it makes less sense not to tell her about the
wedding that evening at a celebratory dinner with Sylvia in attendance.  There,
not only was she not advised of the marriage, but it apparently was also not
mentioned in front of her over the course of the evening.  How does one
celebrate a joyous event without mentioning it?  One can only imagine the verbal
gymnastics required for the toasts.  More to the point, why didn’t Milica find
a way to tell her?

[
123
]

She stated that at the dinner she told a friend of Sylvia about the
wedding, and she “
assumed
” that this friend would tell Sylvia.  That might be true, but the
fact that she would have such information transmitted through a third party,
and that she would not even assure that such person would pass the message on, speaks
volumes about the degree of disconnect, and disrespect between the two women.

[
124
]

This antipathy, at least on Milica’s part, carried over to Professor
Boss’s dying days.  When it was clear that he was approaching death, Milica did
agree to allow Sylvia to see him, but with conditions.  Here is what she wrote
to Caroline Dieluweit on March 27, 2015:

We
really are reaching an end. It would be an appropriate time to inform Sylvia and
to tell her that if she wishes to visit her father to

say good-bye, that
this would be possible,
but under supervision
.

If you find this too difficult to do yourself, please let me
know and I will find an alternative.
[52]

(The
Court’s emphasis)

[
125
]

Sylvia was eventually advised of the possibility to say good-bye to
her father by someone else and her last meeting with him finally did occur.  It
took place at the Parkinson’s treatment centre frequented by Professor Boss,
under supervision.

[
126
]

Élise Thérèse Leduc
, a neighbour who had
babysat Sylvia throughout her youth,  declares the following in her affidavit
dated September 19, 2019:

6.   Effectivement,
j’étais présente à l’été 2004 après l’hospitalisation de Sylvia (après qu'elle
avait entamé ses études en droit à l'Université McGill) parce que je faisais
partie de ceux qui la soutenaient à se remettre de son épisode. Je peux
confirmer que Milica ne lui a jamais adressé ni un seul mot de réconfort ou d'encouragement.

7.   Ce
même été, pendant l'épisode bipolaire ou Sylvia a commis une erreur financière

du tout ».

[
127
]

As mentioned above, Milica seeks to discredit Ms. Leduc’s testimony
by alluding to her possible senility in 2013 and, therefore, at the time she signed

said, the key element in Ms. Leduc’s affidavit is the declaration at paragraph
7 to the effect that Milica stated that Sylvia did not deserve to inherit
anything.  There was no clear denial of this by Milica and, even if there were,
the Court would prefer Ms. Leduc’s evidence on this point.

[
128
]

Caroline Dieluweit
’s privileged position
in the Boss family makes her evidence particularly relevant on this subject,
among others.  She was asked in cross-examination what she meant in paragraph

manipulated me for her own personal gain
”.  Her response was that Milica had told her that “
Sylvia should not inherit any money
”.

[
129
]

Ms. Dieluweit provides numerous details of her observations while
living with the couple and it is worth repeating several of the paragraphs of
her affidavit here:

as I can tell, this very good and supportive father-daughter relationship was
undermined and discouraged by Militsa Krivokapic-Boss. I saw this in Militsa's consistent

[…]

13. I was
told by Militsa that it was Sylvia who did not want to see Valya, and I believed,

used Sylvia's mental health problems to create a negative image of Sylvia's

[
130
]

In cross-examination, she testified that Milica’s depiction of
Sylvia was much more negative than the reality that she eventually came to
learn.  For example, she stated that Milica continuously talked of bipolar

medication, which made it impossible to communicate with her.  Ms. Dieluweit
noted that Professor Boss never stood up to Milica and kept his mouth closed.  Later,
after reaching out to Sylvia, Ms. Dieluweit discovered that she was “
a normal person
”.

[
131
]

There is also the fact that several sources indicate that Milica
felt that Sylvia’s difficult behaviour was harmful to Professor Boss’s health.
This is confirmed by Ms. Dieluweit, who testified that Milica told her that she
confirmed to his doctors that Sylvia was a constant threat to her husband’s
health.

[
132
]

That Sylvia’s comportment could have been prejudicial to her
father’s health might well have been true, for what parent would not be
affected by the type of situations that Sylvia’s illness brought on.  That
being said, it is not relevant for our purposes.  What does play a role,
however, is the fact that Milica held this against Sylvia and blamed her for her
husband’s worsening physical state.

[
133
]

This is reflected in Ms. Dieluweit’s testimony concerning Milica’s “
consistent negative portrayal of Sylvia as
an irresponsible and dangerous person
”, which served to
undermine the father-daughter relationship.  She is not competent to say that this
did, in fact, undermine the relationship, but her testimony does indicate,
contrary to Milica’s affirmations, that Milica’s criticisms were made in Professor
Boss’s presence.  That is consistent with an attempt at undue influence.

[
134
]

Jonathan Horsky
, on the other hand,
declares in his affidavit that he “
never heard Milica speak poorly or in any negative fashion about Sylvia
” in front of Professor Boss or a third party and that he never
witnessed, nor could he even imagine, Milica verbally abusing Sylvia.  He was a

[
135
]

Although the Court believes Mr. Horsky’s evidence, it finds Ms.
Dieluweit’s testimony more enlightening.  She is a family member, and people
tend to let their guards down more in front of family than in the presence of

with the couple generally for eight-day stretches every summer from 2009 onwards.

[
136
]

Dr. Simona Badelescu
, a chemist working
at Concordia University, is the mother of one of Sylvia’s long-time friends.
In April 2009, Sylvia was spending the weekend at the Badelescu residence and

5.   J’étais complètement étonnée de
trouver Sylvia au centre d’une scène où elle ne disait rien mais avait l’air

[

]

She confirms in later paragraphs that the woman in question was

”.  This is consistent with Milica’s own testimony to the effect

[
138
]

Sylvia corroborates this testimony and adds that third-party
bystanders who witnessed the outburst called the police, who eventually arrived
on the scene.  Milica denies that this confrontation ever took place.  She says

[
139
]

The Court has trouble understanding the obstacle posed by a leg
injured five or six months previously to an oral dressing down.  In any event,

[
140
]

Kevin Colgan
, an antiques dealer and
friend and former student of Professor Boss, declared in his affidavit that he
had a telephone conversation with Milica in October 2008 during which she “
launched into Sylvia, referring to her
‘ghastly behaviour’
”, adding that “
it was quite an outpouring
”.

[
141
]

Milica dismisses this affiant as a graduate student who never
finished his Master’s Degree.  This is perhaps true, although it is neither in

and Helen, the Court believes the testimony of Mr. Colgan.

[
142
]

Based on the above evidence, the Court concludes that Milica’s
attitude towards Sylvia was extremely negative, to the point of being hostile
and antagonistic.  Again, let us be clear.  Whether or not Sylvia’s
unpredictable and often unacceptable behaviour deserved such animosity is not
the issue.  What is important is whether this evidence shows that Milica would
likely have attempted to have Professor Boss exclude Sylvia from his will.

[
143
]

The proof examined above, and in particular the declarations of two affiants
to the effect that Milica stated to them that Sylvia did not deserve to inherit
any money from her father, supports Sylvia’s allegation that Milica did so
attempt.

3.  MILICA’S ATTITUDE TOWARDS HER OWN
ENTITLEMENT TO INHERIT

[
144
]

There is multiple corroboration for the conclusion that Milica was a
devoted and loving wife to Professor Boss.  No witness even hinted that she was
anything less than fully and unselfishly devoted to his cause, whether professional,
personal or medical.  She helped him with his work, even to the point of supporting
him in his class presentations, assisted him with his apparently voluminous
correspondence and, when the time came, managed every step of his medical
treatments, down to choosing his doctors.  She idolized him and he was clearly
much better off as a result of having her in his life.

[
145
]

In light of the important role that she played in the last two and a
half decades of her husband’s life, it is quite normal that Milica would expect
to receive a significant portion of her husband’s estate after his passing.
One witness provides insight into the extent to which she felt this
entitlement.

[
146
]

Caroline Dieluweit
recounted the
following in her affidavit:

39.    Valya
did manage to keep some independence, for example by not making Militsa the
beneficiary of his pension.  I saw that Militsa was upset about this financial
decision, as she had expected to live off Valentin's pension and receive a
monthly income, or similar.  In a Skype conversation with me, Militsa announced
this while sobbing, and then at the same time brought up that Valya had decided
to give my son, Julian, his Mini Cooper, which she felt was unfair.  Julian
then politely renounced Valya's offer of the car.

[
147
]

Ms. Dieluweit testified that Milica felt that she deserved to have
the car because she was the one taking care of her husband.  As it turns out,
the Will assuaged Milica’s concerns on both fronts.  Under it, she obtains both
the benefits of the pension plan and the Mini Cooper
[53]
.

[
148
]

Considering Ms. Dieluweit’s testimony, it is probable that these
changes in Professor Boss’s intentions resulted from Milica’s lobbying.  They
are a clear example of the influence that she exercised over him in relation to
his estate.

[
149
]

We thus conclude that Milica was ready to attempt to influence her
husband with respect to the contents of the Will when they did not suit her.
As noted, any significant bequest to Sylvia would not have suited her.  Among
other reasons, she likely felt that, in light of her devoted services to him,
she deserved to inherit essentially his full estate.

4.  PROFESSOR BOSS’S WEAKENED COGNITIVE
STATE

[
150
]

Professor Brière speaks of the “
résistance
”
that a testator would be capable of mustering in the face of an effort to
influence him
[54]
.  This is a broad concept, but central to it are both the mental
and the physical capacities of the person.  Professor Boss’s mental capacity is
the primary subject of this section, while his physical capacity will be
considered in the following section, dealing with his dependence on Milica.

[
151
]

As for his cognitive state, it was covered in detail in the section
of this judgment dealing with the capacity to testate.  There, we hold that the evidence is in favour of finding him mentally competent to
execute the Will, but that there was likely some cognitive diminution by
November 2010.  That holding applies equally in this
section.

[
152
]

Thus, it is not necessary to say anything more on the subject now.  We
shall limit our comments, therefore, to a contradiction in the proof that takes
place in this context.

[
153
]

Simon Berrebi
, whom Professor Boss
described in a reference letter for him as “
One of my finest and brightest undergraduate students
in recent years
”
[55]
, declared in his affidavit that he had noticed a certain
degeneration in Professor Boss starting from 2009 onward.  He mentions that Professor
Boss was “
getting skinnier
” and “
would
sometimes tell the same stories several times
” in his classes.
He declared that “
At some
points Militsa taught some of his classes
” and that “
In Spring 2010 or Fall 2010, Militsa asked
(him) to notify her if (Professor Boss) was ever unwell on a day she was not in
class
”.

[
154
]

In spite of her testimony to the effect that she “
didn’t have knowledge of this young man
”, Milica, herself, filed a chain of emails showing that she wrote

warm greetings
, Militsa”
[56]
and on several others signed “
All the best, Militsa for VB
”
[57]
and “

”
[58]
.

[
155
]

These emails are another element that casts doubt on Milica’s

[
156
]

on meetings with students
(Affidavit
of Arthur Reed)

some of his classes
(Affidavit
of Simon Berrebi; Exhibit D-70, page 29/59)
.

157
]

[60]

158
]

(The

159
]

Au contraire

[
160
]

The Court also notes the testimony of
Caroline Dieluweit
, who

was a regular visitor in the Boss home.  At paragraph 11 of her affidavit
she declares that Professor Boss was “
dependent on Milica in his day to day life
”

.  At paragraph 33 she declares:

]

]

last night and his wife

CONCLUSIONS

[
183
]

Does all this lead to a presumption of undue influence?  According
to article 2846 of the Civil Code, a presumption is “
an inference established by law or the court from a
known fact to an unknown fact.
”  In assessing whether a
presumption is justified, a judge is required by article 2849 to “
take only serious, precise and concordant
provisions into consideration
”.

[
184
]

To understand what these three concepts mean in law, we look to the
case of
Longpré v. Thériault
[76]
, where
the Court of Appeal provides the following assistance in this regard:

•

Serious presumptions are those where the
connections between the known fact and the unknown fact are such that the
existence of the former leads one strongly to conclude in the existence of the
latter;

•

Precise presumptions are those where the
conclusion flowing from the known fact leads directly and specifically to the
unknown one, so that it is not reasonably possible to arrive at a different or
contrary result or fact;

•

Concordance
[77]
among presumptions is relevant where there is more than one
presumption at play, in which case, taken together, they are all consistent
with and tend to prove the unknown fact, and it cannot be said that they
contradict or neutralize each other
[78]
.

[
185
]

With respect to the precision criterion, we should note that the
author Ducharme is of the view that the test is one of simple probability,
rather than near certainty.  He argues that it is not necessary for the
presumption to be so strong as to exclude all other possibilities, as long as
the result is probable
[79]
.  Considering that it is rare in the civil side of the law to see a
requirement exceeding that of probability, it is difficult to understand why
that general rule should not apply when assessing the criterion of precision.
The Court supports Professor Ducharme’s view and will apply it in the present
case.

[
186
]

As analyzed above, the evidence leads to the following findings of
fact in relation to the time the Will was executed:

a.

It is surprising and essentially unexplained by
any communication emanating from Professor Boss why he would to all intents and
purposes disinherit Sylvia;

b.

Milica had a strong antipathy towards Sylvia and
felt that she did not deserve to inherit anything from her father;

c.

In contrast to Sylvia’s lack of just entitlement,
Milica felt, in light of her devoted services to her husband, that she deserved
to inherit the major part of his estate;

d.

Although Professor Boss was mentally competent
to execute the Will, there was likely some cognitive diminution by November
2010;

e.

Professor Boss had developed physical and moral
dependency on Milica by the time of the execution of the Will;

f.

Milica played the role of gate-keeper for her
husband’s social contacts, both physical and written;

g.

Milica had knowledge of the great majority of
her husband’s written communication and undoubtedly exercised some control over
it

[
187
]

Milica’s hostility towards Sylvia and her aversion to the idea that
she should inherit anything are strong indicators that she likely pressured her
husband to exclude his daughter from his testament when he otherwise would not
have done so.  The other factors analyzed show both a
modus operandi
and
the facilitating circumstances that are consistent with such an objective.  This
ensemble of concordant facts paves a path that leads to a serious and precise presumption
of undue influence, and that is the Court’s conclusion.

[
188
]

For these reasons, the Court will grant Sylvia’s application and
annul the Will.  However, not only will it not grant costs to Sylvia, it will also
condemn her to pay legal costs to Milica, including the totality of Milica’s
expert’s fees, an amount of $26,043.64
[80]
.  We
make these exceptional orders for the following reasons.

[
189
]

As for the refusal to award costs, the lion’s share of which is in
the form of expert’s fees, the Court feels compelled to sanction Dr. Brock’s

rejection of Dr. Brock’s reports, there can be no reimbursement of the fees charged
for them.  In that light, this ruling turns out to be not so much a sanction as
a logical consequence of the exclusion of the reports.

[
190
]

consider settlement negotiations with Milica.  Her close-mindedness in this
regard was confirmed in the clearest of terms in the response of her lawyer to
the Court’s question on the point.  He seemed almost incredulous that the Cour
would even suggest such a thing.

[
191

the spirit of the Code of Civil Procedure, but also of the letter.  The very
first article of the Code stipulates that “
Parties must consider private prevention and
resolution processes before referring their dispute to the

courts
”.  Sylvia clearly did not respect this duty and she will be refused
court costs as a result.

[
192

As for the order to pay Milica’s expert’s fees, common sense and

The reasons for this ruling are set out above and they apply directly to this
